Mexican Literature. Mexican literature encompasses the rich tradition of Mexican writers whose work grapples with themes of identity, colonialism, revolution, and modernity. In the twentieth century, figures like Octavio Paz and Carlos Fuentes elevated Mexican letters to global significance, blending indigenous intellectual traditions with European modernism. Mexican literature is central to understanding Latin American letters and the postcolonial imagination.

The twentieth-century boom in Mexican literature coincided with the aftermath of the Mexican Revolution, which became a defining subject. Violence, social upheaval, and national identity reshape Mexican prose. Octavio Paz's essays, particularly The Labyrinth of Solitude, provided a philosophical framework for understanding Mexican identity and psychology. Paz theorizes the Mexican as fundamentally solitary and masked. Carlos Fuentes pioneered the modernist novel in Latin America, blending temporal fragmentation with exploration of power and historical consciousness. The Death of Artemio Cruz deconstructs chronology to interrogate history.

Indigenous voices and pre-Columbian intellectual traditions persist in Mexican literature, distinguishing it from European influences. Nahuatl wisdom and Aztec mythology surface even in contemporary fiction. Mexican writers have been central figures in the Latin American literary boom of the nineteen-sixties through nineteen-seventies, alongside figures like García Márquez and Vargas Llosa. The "boom" itself is partly a Mexican phenomenon. The tradition engages with magic realism, psychological introspection, and formal innovation as responses to Mexican historical trauma and complexity. Surrealism feels natural in a literature born from revolution.

Laura Esquivel, Salvador Elizondo, and other contemporary writers extend Mexican literary tradition, exploring gender, desire, and the persistence of pre-modern consciousness in modern life. Mexican literature maintains a dialogue with American literature while resisting cultural dominance. The border itself—geographic and literary—becomes a recurring subject and formal challenge. Octavio Paz is the poet and essayist whose work defined modern Mexican intellectual life. Carlos Fuentes is the novelist who brought Mexican literature to international modernist prominence. The Labyrinth of Solitude is Paz's foundational essay on Mexican identity and psychology. The Death of Artemio Cruz is Fuentes' masterwork of temporal fragmentation and historical reckoning. Modernism is the aesthetic movement Mexican writers transformed and adapted.
